libOpenCOR only needs a subset of LLVM, so we do everything we can to minimise its footprint. This matters most to our WASM version since our Web app dynamically imports it, but our native versions benefit from it too since we merge LLVM into our static library.

To this end, we don't build Clang at all (the package is still called `LLVMClang` since our prebuilt packages are released under that name). Indeed, the only C code that libOpenCOR ever compiles is the code that libCellML generates for a model, which uses a small and well-defined subset of C. So, libOpenCOR compiles it itself: `src/misc/irgenerator.cpp` parses it and generates the LLVM IR that Clang used to generate for it, and `src/misc/compiler.cpp` has LLVM optimise that IR (using the same `-O3` pipeline as Clang) and generate some machine code for it (using LLVM's ORC-based JIT for our native versions, and as a WebAssembly module for our WASM version).

Our WASM version of LLVM is built with size optimisation (`-Oz`) and without RTTI, while our native versions keep LLVM's default release flags so that they compile our models as fast as possible. Every version is built with only the backend of the target for which it generates code, and with the patches in `patches`, which are applied by `applypatches.cmake`:

- `llvm-optional-optimizations.patch` adds a `LLVM_ENABLE_OPTIONAL_OPTIMIZATIONS` option, `ON` by default so that LLVM otherwise builds exactly as it normally would, which compiles out the optimizations that LLVM's default pipelines only perform when given profile data or a vector library (`-fveclib=`), or when enabled through a command-line option (`-mllvm`), none of which we ever do. This doesn't change the optimizations that are performed on our code, but profile data and vector libraries then result in a fatal error, and the command-line options that would enable those optimizations are not available anymore.

Our native shared library and our Python module only export our own symbols (see `src/CMakeLists.txt` and `src/bindings/python/CMakeLists.txt`). This lets the linker remove the parts of LLVM that we don't use. It also means that, on Linux, another copy of LLVM in the same process (e.g., one from another Python module) cannot interpose its symbols with ours, which is what would otherwise make LLVM report that some of its options are registered more than once.

Note that `LLVMWindowsDriver` (which LLVM's ORC-based JIT uses to locate the MSVC toolchain) and `LLVMOption` (which `LLVMWindowsDriver` needs) are needed by our native versions.
